target_customer: Drivers in San Francisco and later other cities who want to contest parking and traffic tickets without time or legal knowledge
problem: Fighting a ticket takes time and expertise though nearly half of tickets are dismissed in court; Fixed let users photograph a ticket and had the app and advocates file the appeal.
business_model: Success fee of 25 percent of the original fine, nothing if the challenge fails
product_category: Consumer legal tech app for contesting tickets

founders.name: David Hegarty
founders.background_notes: Started Fixed after receiving several tickets he believed were wrong (TechCrunch, 2014-01-15 and 2014-07-24).

founders.name: David Sanghera
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder in TechCrunch 2014-01-15; not on the YC page.

exit.reason: Terms undisclosed; the deal was for the technology, not the team, per TechCrunch.

competitors.name: Parkingticket.com
competitors.what: Web based ticket contesting service described as clumsier than a mobile app

competitors.name: ParkingTicketGuys
competitors.what: Web based ticket contesting service described as clumsier than a mobile app

technical_complexity.rationale: A mobile app that gathers evidence and files appeals, with automation against city ticket sites that later proved fragile when Xerox and cities blocked access.

defensibility.rationale: Depended on access to city parking ticket websites; when San Francisco, Oakland and Los Angeles blocked it in 2015 there was no fallback and rivals were web services doing the same job.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Cities and Xerox blocked Fixed from the ticket sites in fall 2015, so the parking business closed; a law firm bought the technology in June 2016.

market_need_then: San Francisco issued about 1.5 million parking tickets a year worth about 100 million dollars and over 3 billion dollars nationwide (TechCrunch); the beta waitlist ballooned and an early beta filled quickly.

branding.brand_signature: Pay only if it wins (25 percent fee)
branding.community_and_virality: Wide press at launch (TechCrunch, NPR, Boing Boing, Daily Dot) and again when cities blocked it (Gizmodo, Techdirt, Sophos).

brand_strength.rationale: Many outlets covered the launch and the city blocking, but sources do not describe logo, voice or community, and the name is a common word.

pivots.why: San Francisco, Oakland and Los Angeles blocked access and Xerox used a third party to block the ticket site; the company lacked resources to fight back

outcome_analysis: Fixed launched in January 2014 as a beta, raised 1.2M in July 2014 and 650K in February 2015, then lost its parking business in fall 2015 when cities and Xerox blocked its access to ticket systems. It refocused on traffic citations and was bought for its technology by law firm Lawgix on June 15, 2016, so the end was a soft landing rather than a shutdown.
notes: Directory status is Inactive while the exit is an acquisition (June 2016), so the two are consistent.
